core.p: **Part (b)**: Explain how Shakespeare presents good and bad kingship **elsewhere in the play**. In your answer you must consider: the qualities of kings; why kingship matters in the play. You should refer to the context of the play. (20 marks)

bullets: **Thesis**: Shakespeare defines kingship through contrast: holy, generous, healing kings against a paranoid tyrant, to celebrate divine-right monarchy for James I and to show that tyranny poisons both the kingdom and the king.
**P1**: Duncan: generous, trusting, holy; his flaw of misjudgement.
**P2**: Macbeth’s tyranny: insecurity, spies, murders; Scotland suffering.
**P3**: Edward and Malcolm: ‘king-becoming graces’; healing touch.
**P4**: restored order; Banquo’s line and James I.

essays.q: Explain how Shakespeare presents good and bad kingship elsewhere in the play.
essays.text:
Shakespeare defines good kingship through contrast, setting the generous, holy rule of Duncan, Edward and Malcolm against Macbeth’s paranoid tyranny. In doing so he celebrates the divine-right monarchy of James I and shows that tyranny destroys both the kingdom and the tyrant.

Duncan embodies the virtues of a good king. He rewards loyalty generously, telling Macbeth ‘I have begun to plant thee, and will labour / To make thee full of growing’; the agricultural metaphor presents the king as a gardener who nurtures his subjects. Even his castle greeting, praising its ‘pleasant seat’, shows a trusting nature. After his murder he is described in sacred terms, ‘The Lord’s anointed temple’, reflecting the Jacobean belief that kings are appointed by God. Yet Shakespeare also gives Duncan a flaw: he admits ‘There’s no art / To find the mind’s construction in the face’ about the traitor Cawdor, then immediately trusts Macbeth, the new Cawdor. Good kingship, the play suggests, needs judgement as well as goodness.

Macbeth’s reign is the opposite. Kingship brings him no security: ‘To be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus’. He rules through fear, keeping a servant ‘fee’d’ in every noble’s house and murdering Banquo and Macduff’s family. Scotland itself suffers; Ross says it ‘cannot / Be called our mother, but our grave’, an image of a nation turned from nurturing to deadly. The imagery of clothing reinforces his illegitimacy: Angus says his title hangs ‘loose about him, like a giant’s robe / Upon a dwarfish thief’. Shakespeare presents tyranny as unnatural, a violation of the Great Chain of Being reflected in the darkness and disorder of nature after Duncan’s death.

In Act 4, Shakespeare offers a direct definition of good kingship. Malcolm lists the ‘king-becoming graces’: ‘justice, verity, temperance, stableness, / Bounty, perseverance, mercy, lowliness, / Devotion, patience, courage, fortitude’. Macbeth possesses almost none of them. The English king, Edward the Confessor, is said to cure the sick with his touch and to have ‘a heavenly gift of prophecy’; this holy, healing king contrasts with Macbeth, who brings sickness to Scotland. The scene would resonate strongly with James I, who also practised ‘touching’ to heal and who wrote about the duties of kings in Basilikon Doron.

The ending restores rightful order. Macduff enters with ‘Th’ usurper’s cursed head’ and hails Malcolm as king; Malcolm promises to act ‘by the grace of Grace’, placing his rule under God. The show of eight kings in Act 4, descended from Banquo, reminds the audience that James I claimed Banquo as his ancestor. Shakespeare thus frames Macbeth’s reign as an unnatural interruption between legitimate kings, warning that tyranny is temporary and self-defeating, while divine-right monarchy, wise, holy and generous, is the natural order to which the kingdom must return.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare defines good kingship through contrast, setting the generous, holy rule of Duncan, Edward and Malcolm against Macbeth’s paranoid tyranny, in order to celebrate the divine-right monarchy of James I and to show that tyranny destroys both the kingdom and the tyrant.
why: **AO1**: a clear argument through contrast, covering four kings.
**AO3**: divine right, Great Chain of Being, Basilikon Doron, the royal touch, Banquo as James’s ancestor.
Imagery of planting, clothing and sickness as connective tissue.

mistakes.r: His misjudgement of character is a flaw.
mistakes.w: Saying Duncan is a perfect king with no flaws.

mistakes.r: It is the play’s clearest definition of kingship.

summary: A full grade 9 part (b) model essay on kingship and tyranny, contrasting Duncan, Edward the Confessor and Malcolm with Macbeth, with context on divine right and James I.

terms.d: Someone who takes a throne illegitimately.
